content_preview.summary: arXiv now limits submitters to two papers per calendar month and three active submissions, citing a surge in AI-assisted submissions that doubled volume in two years.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

The preprint server arXiv has capped how many papers any one person can submit. According to [arXiv's announcement](https://blog.arxiv.org/2026/10/01/updated-rate-limit-policy/), it "now limits submitters to up to two submissions per calendar month, with a limit of three total active submissions at any given time." The post, written by Kat Boboris and dated October 1, 2026, says the policy applies "across all submitters and categories" and describes it as a stopgap while arXiv deter...

editor_notes.content_quality: Clear Briefing (613 words, within 300-800) with Overview, What We Know, Earlier Measures, What We Don't Know and a short Analysis. Well structured; the Analysis is a modest, hedged inference (quota rationing) that follows directly from the FAQ rules.
editor_notes.source_verification: Read both snapshots from disk (gunzip). source-0.html.gz (blog.arxiv.org, 'Fair Moderation, Equitable Access, and AI: arXiv's Updated Rate Limit Policy', by Kat Boboris, October 1st 2026, HTTP 200): confirms verbatim 'arXiv now limits submitters to up to two submissions per calendar month, with a limit of three total active submissions at any given time'; 'As of October 1st, 2026 ... updated rate limiting policy across all submitters and categories as a stopgap'; 9,869 (Sept 2016), 20,569 (Sept 2024), 40,363 this September, 'a new record', 'almost 9,000 support tickets'; submissions doubled in two years; cs.AI 'over 6X increase', other categories doubled; thin papers, 'salami' papers, 'marked increase in dense, AI-written papers'; AI permitted if disclosed; the Dietterich passage is a blockquote with <cite> 'Thomas Dietterich, Distinguished Professor Emeritus, Oregon State University and Chair of the arXiv Editorial Advisory Council' and the article's quote is verbatim (curly apostrophe in moderators' preserved); FAQ items (rejected papers count, all categories, on-hold papers excluded from monthly but counted in active cap of 3 'Since 2024', co-authors unaffected, deleted-before-announcement not counted, 'plan their submissions carefully') all match; 'continue to monitor the effect of this update... modify as needed' verbatim. 'Three active submissions' meaning is correct: three total submissions in the pipeline at any one time (including on-hold ones), a pre-existing 2024 limit that remains in place, distinct from the new two-per-month cap. source-1.html.gz (thenextweb.com, published May 17, 2026, HTTP 200): cited only for the earlier one-year-ban rule and supports exactly that: ban for one year for obvious unchecked AI generation (hallucinated references, leftover chatbot instructions), subsequent submissions must first be accepted by a peer-reviewed journal, 'one-strike' rule, announced by Thomas Dietterich described as 'computer science section chair'. TNW says nothing about the two-per-month cap or the 40,363 figure, and the article does not attribute them to it. Manifest suspicious_patterns is null for both sources; no injection text found. Both fetches were direct (no archive fallback).
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: All specifics trace to the cited sources. Title/summary: the arXiv post does not literally state 'we are capping because of the record 40,363'; it presents the record September figure, the doubling and the cs.AI 6X increase as the motivating context and states the policy is to 'protect the arXiv corpus from a sharp increase in inappropriate submissions'. The title's 'After' is chronological and consistent with the post's framing; it is not an explicit causal claim and is acceptable. AI link: the arXiv post itself says 'Advanced AI tools are helping drive these increases' and cites a marked increase in dense AI-written papers, so the article's 'Cause' bullet ('part of the rise') is sourced and appropriately hedged; the summary's 'citing a surge in AI-assisted submissions' is supported. The article does not claim AI caused all of the volume. Minor nuance: Dietterich is given different titles by the two sources (EAC Chair vs CS section chair); the article attributes each title to its own source correctly.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional; no sensationalism, no AI self-reference.
editor_notes.originality: No existing article on arXiv, preprint volume or arXiv policy found in src/content/articles (checked 2026-08 through 2026-10 for 'arxiv'/'preprint' titles and submissions). New topic.
concerns: Allowlist warning for blog.arxiv.org: the allowlist contains arxiv.org but the subdomain blog.arxiv.org is not matched. The source is arXiv's own official policy announcement (the primary source), so this is an allowlist-coverage gap rather than a credibility problem; warning overridden, no correction needed.

Topic relevance: this is a research-ecosystem story rather than a software/tool story; the AI link is sourced directly by the arXiv post (AI tools driving volume, cs.AI up over 6X), so it is acceptable on topic. Label as Science & Research / research ecosystem rather than AI Models.
recommendations: Where a source does not state a causal link explicitly, prefer wording like 'amid' to 'after' in titles.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Accurate, well-sourced, appropriately hedged Briefing. Every figure, quote and rule verified verbatim against arXiv's own post; the Next Web is cited only for the earlier one-year-ban rule. APPROVE.
